newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish inflation seen 1.5 pct in one year - survey.
newsitem.headline: Swedish inflation seen 1.5 pct in one year - survey.

text.p: Sweden's business sector sees Swedish inflation expectations marginally higher than they did in December, a survey commissioned by the central bank, the Riksbank, showed on Wednesday.
The survey, by economic research institute Prospera AB, showed those surveyed expected Swedish consumer prices to rise 1.5 percent in one year, 1.7 percent in two years and 2.0 percent in five years.
This compares to a similar survey in December when inflation in one year's time was seen at 1.4 percent, in two years at 1.6 percent and in five years at 2.0 percent.
The survey also showed that Swedish wages were expected to rise three percent in one year, 2.9 percent in two years and 2.9 percent in five years.
The one and two year figures were unchanged compared to the last survey while the five year figure was slightly lower than the three percent expected in December.
The survey, of money market players, purchasing managers and representatives of employees' and employers' organisations, is carried out four times a year.
It is considered one of the central bank's key analytical tools used in its policy planning and is considered one of the weightiest in Sweden when it comes to forecasting inflation.
These figures were an average of those surveyed. The group was divided on their forecasts for inflation in the next year and the next two years, Prospera said in a statement.
"Employers and purchasing managers believe in increased, employees in about unchanged and money market players in decreased inflation," it said.
It said the inflationary expectations were lower than the Riksbank's target of two percent inflation with a one percentage point variation in either direction.
"Inflationary expectations are still distinctly below Sweden's Riksbank's goal the next year and the next two years and close to this goal the next five years," it said.
Prospera said a trend of consistently lowered inflationary expectations that has prevailed since its first survey in the autumn of 1995 had been broken.
It also said wage increase expectations had been lowered.
"But it is only the reduction of the employees' next year wage increase expectations that is statistically significant.
"The employers today expect a slight reduction in the annual wage increases. The other categories expect a fairly flat wage increase development," Prospera said.
